newsitem.title: USA: NYC lawmakers consider legalizing tattoos.
newsitem.headline: NYC lawmakers consider legalizing tattoos.

text.p: Anything goes in New York City -- unless you want to tattoo your sweetheart's name on your bicep.
Tattooing is against the law in New York City, but the City Council is weighing a bill that would make the practice legal at long last.

"It's ridiculous. Thousands of people get tattoos every year," said the bill's main sponsor, Councilwoman Kathryn Freed, at a hearing on Tuesday. "Clearly we need some kind of regulation, and the public has the right to feel it is sanitary."

The hearing attracted a crowd of more than 100 tattoo artists and advocates, whose black leather, pierced lips and, of course, elaborate tattoos stood in striking contrast to the Council chambers' elegant oak panelling and gilded mouldings.

"We're basically honest people. We would prefer to be above ground," tattooist Denise de la Cerda told the lawmakers. "The regulations would help us all. It would mean a standard of professionalism in the industry."

While tattoo parlours have been banned in New York City since an outbreak of Hepatitis B in 1961 was traced to the practice, the city is filled with tattoo parlours, particularly in the more bohemian downtown neighbourhoods. The same parlours often offer body piercing and even branding, which are legal.
And tattoo artists freely advertise in the local telephone book, newspaper ads and storefront signs.

Under the proposed bill, tattoists would hvae to pass an examination to acquire a license. The city's Health Department would regulate and inspect tattooists and tattoo parlours, requiring sanitary conditions and proper needle disposal.
No one under 18 years old would be permitted to get a tattoo.

Not all the tattooists at Tuesday's hearing were entirely in favour of moving to the right side of the law. Being legal could mean burdensome regulations and too much competition, said tattooist Darren Rosa.
"On the surface I think it should be legal," Rosa said. "However, I feel New York City has no idea what it is in for."
The council will hold further hearings on the bill and is likely to vote on it next year.
